How These Estimates Are Made

Every estimate on this site comes from the same approach: a model of Hawaiʻi’s taxpayers is taxed under current law and again under the proposed change, and the difference between the two is the estimate. Each estimate’s page ends with its own detailed method and the data needed to check it.

Building the Model

No one publishes every Hawaiʻi tax return, so the model uses a stand-in of about 40,000 households and individuals drawn from the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, which records income, family type, age and where people live, and adjusted until its totals match what the Department of Taxation reports for the state. Because surveys miss most people with incomes above $1 million, who pay a large share of the income tax, those filers are added from IRS and Department of Taxation statistics, and each household’s income is then grown year by year with Congressional Budget Office projections, out to tax years 2027 through 2031.

The model then computes each household’s tax under current law and again under the proposal, using the statute’s own rates, brackets, deductions and credit schedules. The estimate is the difference, added up across the state and by income group, which shows who would pay more or less as well as the total.

Behavior and Checks

People also respond to changes in the tax code. Not everyone who qualifies for a credit claims it, so the model sets each credit’s claim rate to match what the Department of Taxation actually paid out and holds that rate fixed. When tax rates rise, high earners tend to report less taxable income and a few move away, which the model builds in. A household that leaves costs the state all of the tax it would have paid, which is more than the increase alone.

The model is also tested against Department of Taxation figures that it was not fitted to. In 2022, before the credits were expanded, the credits model comes within 2 percent of what the Department paid.

These are estimates, not predictions. They depend on assumptions, and the ones that move the results most, such as how much high earners cut their reported income when rates rise, are stated on each page, with ranges where they matter. The conveyance tax estimate works differently, from county records of home sales, and its page explains how. The code, data and every setting behind each figure are public, and each page lets readers download the numbers.
